clue.text: Lover in government leaving note - feeling the pressure

indicators.note: what leaves a word walks out of it, so the scrap named next is subtracted from the letters assembled so far

blocks.note: the word for a man's lover on the side, and it is about to lose its first two letters
MI is a note of the sol-fa scale, and those are the two letters that go
the little word is taken at face value, two letters straight from the clue
G is the abbreviation for government, the G of G-men

explanation.walkthrough: The surface promises a Westminster affair, and the dash is where it stops: everything before it is letters. Sol-fa gives a setter do, re, mi, fa, so, la and te as ready-made two-letter scraps.
explanation.definitionFit: feeling the pressure -> STRESSING: the informal verb for being under strain, as in 'don't stress' — mental load rather than physical force.

clue.text: Terminus open in Telford deserted surprisingly

indicators.note: a deserted town has emptied out its middle, so only the letters standing at either end are left
something that turns out surprisingly has not come out in the order you were expecting, which is what these letters do

blocks.note: six letters of fodder, taken straight from the clue
the outside letters of the Shropshire new town, its middle abandoned

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a train leaving a Midlands town, which is exactly what the definition wants you to picture; Telford is only there for its first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Terminus -> END POINT: the place where a line or a journey stops, the same sense as a railway terminus, spelled out as two plain words.

clue.text: Teacher's wig sent up by third of students

indicators.note: in a down entry, anything sent up climbs back towards the first square, so the piece is read bottom to top
the third of a word is the letter you land on counting three in from its start

blocks.note: a rug is slang for a hairpiece, and these three letters climb the entry
counting three letters into students lands on this one

explanation.walkthrough: Wig, teacher and students all belong to the same schoolroom picture, and only one of the three words is the definition — the other two are hair and a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Teacher -> GURU: the Sanskrit word for a spiritual teacher, borrowed into English for any revered expert whose followers hang on the advice.

clue.text: Charismatic female working with computers?

definitions.note: The definition says what she does rather than naming what she is, and the question mark admits the joke: read literally, the two words describe a woman employed in information technology.

blocks.note: 'it' is the old word for sex appeal and star quality, the thing Clara Bow was said to have
the everyday word for a young female, four letters as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is the setter owning up: the phrase really names a charismatic socialite, and only the literal reading sends her to a keyboard. IT for sex appeal dates from the silent films.
explanation.definitionFit: working with computers? -> IT GIRL: IT is information technology, so the phrase read straight names a woman in that trade — the whimsy the question mark flags.

clue.text: Can love tailless bird

indicators.note: a creature with no tail is missing what comes at its very back, so the word gives up its final letter

blocks.note: a tin is a can, the food container
amour is French for love, and its closing R is the tail that goes

explanation.walkthrough: Three short words and no obvious instruction: 'tailless' is the only signal, and it is pointing at a French word rather than an English one. The bird itself is a South American ground-dweller, a cousin of the rheas.
explanation.definitionFit: bird -> TINAMOU: definition by example, one partridge-like species of South America clued only by its family — the standard courtesy with an obscure creature.

clue.text: Working times are reduced for distinguished practitioners

indicators.note: to work a material is to knead and push it out of shape, so the letters will not stay in the shape they arrive in
a word reduced is made shorter, and the standard cut takes the letter off the end

blocks.note: five letters of fodder, straight from the clue
the word are, cut short, its final E left out of the mix

explanation.walkthrough: 'Working times are reduced' is a whole sentence about shift patterns, which is why nothing in it looks like fodder. The answer is the Italian plural of maestro, which is why it ends in I where English would want an S.
explanation.definitionFit: distinguished practitioners -> MAESTRI: masters of an art, usually conductors, and Italian keeps its own plural of maestro when English borrows the word.

clue.text: Count time mother's without

indicators.note: the older sense is on the outside of — the walls without the city — so the word named goes round the piece, not away from it

blocks.note: mater is Latin for mother and British public-school slang for one's mum; it opens up after two letters
T is the standard abbreviation for time, as in the physics formula

explanation.walkthrough: Two traps in six words: 'Count' is the verb and not the nobleman, and 'without' is the archaic outside-of sense rather than an instruction to take something away.
explanation.definitionFit: Count -> MATTER: the verb sense of counting, as in 'it doesn't count' — to carry weight or importance, not to enumerate.

clue.text: Comes across English baseball team outside

indicators.note: a piece told to stand outside wraps round the one beside it instead of joining on at either end

blocks.note: the New York Mets are a Major League club, and the name splits after its first letter
E is the usual abbreviation for English

explanation.walkthrough: An American sport in a British paper is normal service: a four-letter ball club is as standard a piece of crossword furniture as ANT is for a worker.
explanation.definitionFit: Comes across -> MEETS: the sense of running into somebody by chance, in the same third-person singular, not the other sense of making an impression.

clue.text: Horny African shaking rear in style

indicators.note: an animal shaking its back end is losing what sits right at the back, which for a word is its final letter

blocks.note: a large spiral-horned antelope of southern Africa, five letters of it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Horny' sets up a joke the clue never delivers: the horns belong to an antelope. French supplies the answer, as it usually does for words about dash and flair.
explanation.definitionFit: style -> ELAN: the French loan for dash and verve, doing something with visible energy, rather than style as fashion or as a manner of writing.

clue.text: Gather agent's hiding 10% from accountant

indicators.note: what an agent hides is kept within, so the letter goes inside the word rather than beside it
accountant is a ten-letter word, so a tenth of it is a single letter — the one it starts with

blocks.note: a rep is an agent, the sales or theatrical kind, and it opens after two letters
a tenth of a ten-letter word is one letter, and it is taken from the start

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an agent taking commission, and ten per cent is exactly what an agent takes — the joke is that the percentage is arithmetic done on the word, not on the money.
explanation.definitionFit: Gather -> REAP: the harvest verb, cutting and collecting a crop, extended to gathering whatever your efforts earn — you reap what you sow.

clue.text: Clue (1ac) solved - people involved promoting co-operation

indicators.note: a puzzle is solved when its pieces end up in an arrangement other than the one you were handed
people who get involved are mixed in among the others rather than left standing at one end

blocks.note: there is no 1 across in this grid, so the bracket is not a cross-reference: it is Roman one plus the abbreviation for across, tacked on to the four letters before it
men are people, three more letters for the mix

explanation.walkthrough: Look at the numbering before you go hunting: this grid has no 1 across, which is the fair warning that the bracket is letters. Ecumenical began as a church word for unity between denominations.
explanation.definitionFit: promoting co-operation -> ECUMENICAL: first used of Christian churches working together, now of any effort to unite groups that normally keep apart.

clue.text: Dolly Parton's behind first benefit

blocks.note: the American word for a backside; naming a Tennessee country singer is how the clue asks for the American one rather than the British
first written as an ordinal is 1st, and Roman one plus that two-letter ending spells it

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is rude and the parse is not. Parton is in the clue for her nationality rather than her fame, and 1st is a standard three letters once the numeral is read as Roman.
explanation.definitionFit: benefit -> ASSIST: the verb sense, to do somebody good by helping them along, the way a subsidy or a spare pair of hands benefits whoever gets it.

clue.text: Rock chick shortly gets back in club

indicators.note: a word put shortly is cut short, and the cut takes its last letter
in an across entry a piece that gets back is read from the right, so its letters arrive in the opposite order
a piece placed in something sits between its letters rather than alongside them

blocks.note: a bat is a club you swing, and it splits after two letters
a chick is informally a lass, here docked of its final letter and then turned round

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock chick' reads as one phrase and is two jobs: the definition stops after the first word, and the chick is fodder. The music-club surface is entirely a decoy.
explanation.definitionFit: Rock -> BASALT: definition by example — the dark volcanic rock of the Giant's Causeway is one kind of rock, clued by the general word.

clue.text: One narrow-minded old priest, ultimately under grown-up

indicators.note: what comes ultimately comes at the very end, so the word gives up only its final letter
in a down entry what is under something is written below it, so these pieces sit after the word named last

blocks.note: a grown-up is a big person, the way a small child puts it
O is the standard abbreviation for old
the closing letter of the word priest, taken on its own

explanation.walkthrough: The definition is 'One narrow-minded' — a person, not the quality — and the rest of the sentence is three separate scraps dressed up as a remark about the clergy.
explanation.definitionFit: One narrow-minded -> BIGOT: someone who holds an opinion so tightly that no argument reaches them, named here by the trait instead of the label.

clue.text: Mention about upsetting kind of acid

indicators.note: to upset something is to tip it over, and in a down entry that means the letters are read from the bottom up

blocks.note: to cite something is to mention it, four letters that will be read the other way
ca. is short for circa, Latin for about, the abbreviation put before an approximate date

explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration says six because the answer is split over two entries, 13 and 16 down. It is the acid that makes vinegar sour.
explanation.definitionFit: kind of acid -> ACETIC: the acid of vinegar, from Latin acetum; the definition names the family and leaves the wordplay to pick which member.

clue.text: Bones in state - one arm shattered

indicators.note: something shattered has broken into pieces that no longer sit in the order they were in

blocks.note: five letters of fodder, taken as they stand
one is the Roman numeral I, the crossword's usual single letter for it
three more letters of fodder

explanation.walkthrough: The bones are in the foot, so 'arm' is pure misdirection, and 'state' looks as if it wants to be an abbreviation. The Latin plural of metatarsus ends in -i.
explanation.definitionFit: Bones -> METATARSI: the long bones of the foot between the ankle and the toes, in the Latin plural that anatomy keeps.

clue.text: Garment manufacturers designed kit with tennis legend

indicators.note: something designed has been deliberately put together out of parts, which is the licence to arrange these letters into a new shape

blocks.note: three letters of fodder, straight from the clue
twelve more letters — no particular champion is wanted, just the two words themselves

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tennis legend' begs you to name a player, and Borg, Laver and Evert all suit the surface; the clue only ever wanted the twelve letters of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Garment manufacturers -> KNITTING NEEDLES: the tools are credited with making the jumper, a whimsical plural definition by what the pair turns out.

clue.text: See 13
Rene not swimming in canal

indicators.note: letters that are swimming are drifting about with no fixed order, the sense of a head swimming

blocks.note: a French given name, four letters of fodder
three more letters, taken as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Canal' wants to be water, and Rene and swimming both push you towards a French waterway. It is the anatomical sense instead: the gut.
explanation.definitionFit: canal -> ENTERON: the anatomical sense, the alimentary canal or gut of an animal, biology's word for the digestive tube rather than a waterway.

clue.text: Wife and husband European

blocks.note: in Cockney slang a man's wife is his old dutch, from the music-hall song
a woman's man is her husband, as in 'my man'

explanation.walkthrough: Cockney slang and plain English sit side by side with nothing to mark which is which — a fairness a British solver never notices and everyone else has to be told.
explanation.definitionFit: European -> DUTCHMAN: definition by example, a man from the Netherlands being one European among many, with the wordplay left to say which.

clue.text: Cope with success that's netted Bill a thousand

indicators.note: to net something is to catch it and hold it inside, so the pieces named land within the word before them

blocks.note: a hit is a success, a record or a show that lands, and it opens after its first letter
a bill is an account, and a/c is the standard abbreviation for one
K is a thousand, the kilo prefix used of salaries and file sizes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cope with success' reads as one phrase, and the definition stops at the first word. The capital letter on Bill is the other trap: it is a piece of paper, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Cope -> HACK IT: the informal phrase for managing under pressure, since 'can't hack it' says exactly what 'can't cope' says, object and all.

clue.text: Aftershave at first was effective round female? Not much

indicators.note: what a word is at first is the letter it begins with, and that single letter is all the fragment hands over

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word aftershave
a remark that bit was one that took effect — the past tense of bite
O is the round letter, the one drawn as a circle
F is the standard abbreviation for female

explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' looks like an instruction to put one piece outside another, and here it is only the shape of a letter. The rest of the clue is four scraps in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: Not much -> A BIT OF: the phrase measures out a small quantity, as in 'a bit of trouble' — an idiom rather than a one-word synonym.

clue.text: Tory leader drops one point - neat

indicators.note: someone who drops something lets it fall away, so the letter named is no longer in the word

blocks.note: Kemi Badenoch leads the Conservative Party, whose members are the Tories, and her first name supplies four letters
one is the Roman numeral I, and that is the letter dropped
pt is the abbreviation for point, as on a compass or a scoreboard

explanation.walkthrough: 'Tory leader' looks like an instruction to take the first letter of Tory; it is the politician herself. The answer survives in ordinary English mainly as the opposite of unkempt.
explanation.definitionFit: neat -> KEMPT: tidy and well groomed, the positive form that unkempt was built from and that now sounds odd standing alone.

clue.text: Turkey meal comes round with dinners originally for four

indicators.note: a piece that comes round another goes about it, opening up to let the other sit inside
a word taken originally gives up only the letter it starts with

blocks.note: tea is a meal in Britain, the one eaten in the early evening, and it opens after two letters
TR is Turkey's international vehicle registration code, the oval sticker on the back of a car
the first letter of dinners

explanation.walkthrough: Turkey, meal and dinners in one sentence make a Christmas picture, and not one of them is food: a country code, a container and an initial.
explanation.definitionFit: four -> TETRAD: a group of four things taken together, from the Greek tetra-, so the bare number stands for the set it counts.

clue.text: Nothing you said that's wrong or not genuine

indicators.note: a letter that is said is being named aloud, so what you write down is the single character and what you hear is its name

blocks.note: sweet FA is British slang for nothing at all — Fanny Adams, put politely
the name of this letter is the word you, so saying it aloud is worth one character
a cross in the margin is what marks an answer wrong

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is somebody conceding an argument — nothing you said was wrong — and the parse breaks it into three unrelated scraps, one of them a polite piece of slang.
explanation.definitionFit: not genuine -> FAUX: French for false, used in English of deliberate imitations — faux fur, faux leather — where the fake is admitted rather than passed off.

clue.text: Wearing headphones, I stick around for late-starting Sky feature

indicators.note: what you wear goes on you, so the letter named is put inside the thing being worn
a piece told to go around turns about, and comes out read in the other direction
a word that starts late has not begun by its first letter, so that letter never appears

blocks.note: cans is studio slang for headphones, and the word opens before its last letter
the pronoun is taken at face value, one letter lifted from the clue
to jam is to stick fast, and these three letters are then read backwards
the word for, without the F it starts with

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sky feature' is all the clue says about the Great Dog, the constellation that carries Sirius. 'Late-starting' is the device worth keeping: a word that begins one letter in.
explanation.definitionFit: Sky feature -> CANIS MAJOR: a constellation is a feature of the night sky, and this is the Great Dog that follows Orion across it.

clue.text: Lift up ball on green

blocks.note: the garage verb, what you do to a car with a hydraulic prop under the sill
in lawn bowls the small white target ball is rolled out first and the woods are aimed at it

explanation.walkthrough: Five words, no indicator, nothing to take apart — the tell is that no word in the clue asks you to do anything. Bowls is played on a green, which is what makes the second half fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Lift up -> JACK: the verb for raising a car on a screw prop; ball on green -> JACK: the little white target ball in lawn bowls.

clue.text: Pick up from the armourer's

indicators.note: the answer is to be taken from the words that follow, which are carrying it letter for letter

blocks.note: the letters run consecutively across the gap between these two words

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing announces the hiding place but 'from', which is why this one works: the span runs straight over a space, and the eye reads spaces as boundaries.
explanation.definitionFit: Pick up -> HEAR: the sense of catching a sound — 'I didn't pick that up' means it was not heard — rather than lifting or collecting.

clue.text: To demand money with threats no longer wrong

blocks.note: an ex- anything is what it no longer is: ex-wife, ex-president
a tort is a civil wrong in law, the sort you sue over rather than prosecute

explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs to five words and the wordplay to two, which is a shape worth recognising: when a clue reads like a dictionary entry, the parse is hiding at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To demand money with threats -> EXTORT: the verb for getting money by intimidation, blackmail's more general name, in the infinitive the clue offers.

clue.text: May very stupid person attempt to influence voters?

blocks.note: may and can are the two words for being permitted
v is the abbreviation for very, as in v good
an ass is a fool, by way of the donkey

explanation.walkthrough: The capital M wants to be a month or a prime minister, and it is only the plain verb 'may'. Canvassing is the doorstep work candidates do before polling day.
explanation.definitionFit: attempt to influence voters -> CANVASS: to canvass is to go round soliciting votes, so the definition names the whole business rather than one part of it.
